slides.heading: Why did war return in 1939?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the **long-term causes** and the **immediate cause** of the Second World War.

slides.narration: Only twenty years after the peace of nineteen nineteen, the world was at war again. Why? In this part we look at German anger over the peace treaty, the rise of dictators, the policy of appeasement, aggression in Asia and Africa, and finally the invasion of Poland, which started the war.

slides.narration: This timeline gives the main dates of the chapter. Japan seized Manchuria in nineteen thirty-one. Germany moved into the Rhineland in nineteen thirty-six and took Austria and the Sudetenland in nineteen thirty-eight. The war began in nineteen thirty-nine, and ended in nineteen forty-five, after which two new alliances divided Europe.

slides.heading: Dissatisfaction with Versailles
slides.body_md: German anger over the **peace of 1919**.

rows: Blamed Germany alone for the war

visual.alt: Table of terms of 1919 that Germans resented: the war-guilt clause, reparations, loss of Alsace-Lorraine, the Polish Corridor and colonies, and the small army

slides.narration: Many Germans hated the peace treaty of nineteen nineteen. It blamed Germany alone for the war, demanded heavy payments, took away land and colonies, and left only a small army. During the hard years that followed, Hitler promised to tear up the treaty, and this promise won him wide support.

slides.heading: Quick check: the Axis
slides.body_md: Which agreement of 1936 brought Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany together?
slides.narration: Two dictators drew together in nineteen thirty-six. Which agreement linked them?

slides.heading: The rise of the dictators
slides.body_md: **Mussolini**, **Hitler** and a **military-led Japan**.

rows: Glory through expansion, as in Abyssinia
Empire in East Asia, beginning with China

visual.alt: Table of the aggressive powers: Italy under Mussolini from 1922 seeking expansion; Germany under Hitler from 1933 seeking to overturn Versailles, rearm and expand; Japan under a military-led government in the 1930s seeking an empire in East Asia

slides.narration: In Italy, Mussolini set up a Fascist dictatorship in the nineteen twenties. In Germany, Hitler and the Nazis took power in nineteen thirty-three. Both glorified force, rearmed and wanted new territory, and in nineteen thirty-six they drew together. In Japan, military leaders pushed for an empire in East Asia.

slides.heading: Appeasement, step by step
slides.body_md: Britain and France **gave way** in the hope of keeping peace.

nodes.label: September 1938: Munich gives the Sudetenland to Germany

visual.alt: Flow of appeasement: the Rhineland remilitarised in 1936 with no action; the Anschluss in March 1938; Munich giving the Sudetenland to Germany in September 1938; the rest of Czechoslovakia occupied in March 1939; Britain and France then guarantee Poland
visual.caption: Each step encouraged the next.

slides.narration: Britain and France followed appeasement, giving in to some of Hitler's demands. They did nothing when German troops entered the Rhineland in nineteen thirty-six or when Germany swallowed Austria in nineteen thirty-eight. At Munich they agreed to hand him the Sudetenland. When he seized the rest of Czechoslovakia in nineteen thirty-nine, the policy collapsed.

slides.heading: Quick check: Munich
slides.body_md: True or false: under the Munich Agreement of 1938, Germany was allowed to take the Sudetenland.
slides.narration: Recall what the four leaders decided at Munich in nineteen thirty-eight.

slides.heading: Why appeasement? Two views
columns:
**Reasons it was followed**

- Horror of another war like **1914–18**
- Britain and France **not ready** to fight
- Some felt German grievances were **partly fair**

**Why critics condemned it**

- Each concession **encouraged** further demands
- **Czechoslovakia** was sacrificed
- It made the **USSR** distrust the West
slides.narration: Compare the two views. Supporters of appeasement remembered the horror of the last war, knew their countries were not ready to fight, and felt some German complaints were fair. Critics said every concession only encouraged further demands, that Czechoslovakia was sacrificed, and that the Soviet Union came to distrust the West.

slides.heading: The League of Nations fails
slides.body_md: **Manchuria**, **Abyssinia** and **China**.

visual.alt: Table of the League's failures: Manchuria in 1931, where Japan was condemned and left the League in 1933; Abyssinia in 1935, where Italy faced weak sanctions without an oil ban and completed its conquest; and China in 1937, where the League took no effective action

slides.narration: The League of Nations could not stop aggression. When Japan seized Manchuria in nineteen thirty-one, the League condemned it, and Japan simply left. When Italy invaded Abyssinia in nineteen thirty-five, the sanctions were weak and did not include oil. In nineteen thirty-seven Japan began a full war in China.

slides.heading: Poland: the immediate cause
slides.body_md: From the **pact** to the **declarations** of war.

nodes.label: 3 September 1939: Britain and France declare war

visual.alt: Flow of the outbreak of war: the Nazi-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact on 23 August 1939, Germany invading Poland on 1 September, and Britain and France declaring war on 3 September 1939
visual.caption: Eleven days that began the war.

slides.narration: On the twenty-third of August nineteen thirty-nine, Germany and the Soviet Union agreed not to attack each other. Freed from the fear of a war on two fronts, Hitler invaded Poland on the first of September. Two days later, on the third of September, Britain and France declared war on Germany.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: long-term and immediate causes
slides.body_md: Sort the causes into **two** groups.
bullets: Step 1: the **spark** is the invasion of **Poland**.
Step 2: the **fuel** is Versailles, dictators, appeasement, aggression and the League's failure.
Tip: never write that one event alone caused the war.

rows: Japanese and Italian aggression; failure of the League

visual.alt: Table separating long-term causes, namely resentment of Versailles, dictatorships, appeasement, Japanese and Italian aggression and the League's failure, from the immediate cause, the German invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939

slides.narration: Practise sorting causes. The immediate cause, the spark, was the invasion of Poland on the first of September nineteen thirty-nine. The long-term causes, the fuel, were German resentment of Versailles, the dictators, appeasement, aggression by Japan and Italy, and the failure of the League. Always keep the two groups separate.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: resentment of Versailles helps Hitler; dictators glorify force and form the Axis; appeasement over the Rhineland, Austria and Munich; the League fails over Manchuria, Abyssinia and China; Poland is invaded on 1 September 1939
visual.caption: Part 1 in five lines.

slides.narration: To sum up Part One. Resentment of the peace of nineteen nineteen helped Hitler rise. Dictators in Italy and Germany glorified force and drew together. Appeasement let Germany grow stronger, and the League failed to stop Japan and Italy. The invasion of Poland on the first of September nineteen thirty-nine began the war.

slides.heading: From world war to cold war
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **Pearl Harbour**, **Hiroshima and Nagasaki**, the **results** of the war and the **Cold War**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: Pearl Harbour in 1941, Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945, defeat of the Axis, the United Nations in 1945, and the Cold War with NATO in 1949 and the Warsaw Pact in 1955
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we follow the war as it spread across the world, see how it ended in nineteen forty-five, and study its results. Then we meet a new kind of conflict, the Cold War, in which the two strongest powers competed without fighting each other directly.

slides.heading: Pearl Harbour, 7 December 1941
slides.body_md: The attack that brought the **USA** into the war.

rows: American naval base at Pearl Harbour, Hawaii
The USA entered the war; it became a world war

visual.alt: Table about Pearl Harbour: on 7 December 1941 Japan attacked the American naval base at Pearl Harbour in Hawaii, and the USA entered the war, which became a world war

slides.narration: On the seventh of December nineteen forty-one, Japanese aircraft attacked the American naval base at Pearl Harbour in Hawaii. The United States, which had stayed out of the war, now declared war on Japan, and Germany and Italy declared war on the United States. The conflict became a true world war.

slides.heading: Two sides in a world war
slides.body_md: The **Axis** against the **Allies** after 1941.

rows: Europe, North Africa, Asia and the Pacific
Britain, the USSR (from 1941), the USA (from December 1941), China and others
Europe, North Africa, Asia and the Pacific

visual.alt: Table of the two sides: the Axis of Germany, Italy and Japan, and the Allies including Britain, the USSR from 1941, the USA from December 1941 and China, fighting across Europe, North Africa, Asia and the Pacific
visual.caption: The two sides after 1941.

slides.narration: By the end of nineteen forty-one the two sides were clear. The Axis powers were Germany, Italy and Japan. Against them stood the Allies, including Britain, the Soviet Union, which Germany had invaded in nineteen forty-one, the United States and China. Fighting now stretched from Europe and North Africa to Asia and the Pacific.

slides.heading: How the war ended
slides.body_md: **Germany** in May 1945; **Japan** after the atomic bombs.

visual.alt: Flow of the end of the war: Germany surrenders in May 1945; an atomic bomb falls on Hiroshima on 6 August and on Nagasaki on 9 August 1945; Japan surrenders in August to September 1945
visual.caption: How the war ended.

slides.narration: The war in Europe ended when Germany surrendered in May nineteen forty-five. In Asia, the United States dropped atomic bombs on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima on the sixth of August and Nagasaki on the ninth of August. The bombs caused very heavy loss of life, and Japan surrendered soon after.

slides.body_md: On which Japanese city was the first atomic bomb dropped, on 6 August 1945?
slides.narration: Two cities were struck in August nineteen forty-five. Which was the first?

slides.heading: Consequences of the war
slides.body_md: **Axis defeated**, the **United Nations**, two **superpowers**.

rows: Germany, Italy and Japan defeated; Germany occupied
The Cold War between the two blocs

visual.alt: Table of consequences of the war: the Axis defeated and Germany occupied; the United Nations founded on 24 October 1945; the USA and USSR as superpowers; and the Cold War between two blocs

slides.narration: The war changed the world. Germany, Italy and Japan were defeated, and Germany was occupied. To keep the peace, the United Nations came into existence on the twenty-fourth of October nineteen forty-five. Britain and France were weakened, while the United States and the Soviet Union rose as the two superpowers.

slides.heading: What was the Cold War?
slides.body_md: Rivalry **without** a direct war.

rows: The two superpowers never fought each other in a full-scale war
Competition in nuclear and other weapons
Each side spread its own ideas and attacked the other

visual.alt: Table of Cold War features: no direct war between the superpowers, an arms race, propaganda, and rival alliances, NATO in 1949 and the Warsaw Pact in 1955

slides.narration: After the war, the two superpowers, once allies, became rivals. The United States stood for capitalism and multi-party democracy, the Soviet Union for communism. Their contest is called the Cold War because they never fought each other in a full-scale war. Instead they competed through weapons, propaganda and alliances.

slides.narration: Europe was divided into two camps. The western countries, led by the United States, stood on one side; the Soviet Union and the communist states of eastern Europe stood on the other. Each bloc feared the other, and each built up its armed strength.

slides.heading: NATO and the Warsaw Pact
slides.body_md: **NATO (1949)** and the **Warsaw Pact (1955)**: meaning only.

rows: Western military alliance for mutual defence
Military alliance of the USSR and eastern European communist states

visual.alt: Table of the two Cold War alliances: NATO, 1949, led by the USA, a western military alliance for mutual defence; and the Warsaw Pact, 1955, led by the USSR, a military alliance of communist states of eastern Europe
visual.caption: Meaning only, as the syllabus requires.

slides.narration: Each bloc formed a military alliance. In nineteen forty-nine the United States, Canada and western European countries formed the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, promising to defend one another. In nineteen fifty-five the Soviet Union and the communist states of eastern Europe answered with the Warsaw Pact.

slides.heading: Quick check: which alliance?
slides.body_md: True or false: the USSR was a member of NATO.

notes.title: The Second World War and the Cold War — notes

sections.heading: 1. Versailles and the rise of the dictators
sections.body_md:
- **Versailles (1919):** war guilt, reparations, lost land and a small army left Germans bitter; they saw it as a dictated peace.
- **Mussolini** (Italy, from **1922**) and **Hitler** (Germany, from **1933**) built dictatorships that glorified force, rearmed and wanted new land.
- **Rome–Berlin Axis (1936):** Italy and Germany drew together; **Japan** later joined them. The three became the **Axis** powers.

key_terms.definition_md: Germany, Italy and Japan, the aggressor states of the Second World War.
A settlement imposed on the defeated side without negotiation.

rows: Blamed Germany alone for the war

visual.alt: Table of terms of 1919 that Germans resented: the war-guilt clause, reparations, loss of Alsace-Lorraine, the Polish Corridor and colonies, and the small army

rows: Glory through expansion, as in Abyssinia
Empire in East Asia, beginning with China

visuals.alt: Table of the aggressive powers: Italy under Mussolini from 1922 seeking expansion; Germany under Hitler from 1933 seeking to overturn Versailles, rearm and expand; Japan under a military-led government in the 1930s seeking an empire in East Asia

sections.heading: 2. Appeasement
sections.body_md:
- **Meaning:** satisfying an aggressor's demands in the hope of avoiding war; followed by **Britain** and **France** towards Hitler.
- **Steps:** Rhineland remilitarised (**1936**); **Anschluss** with Austria (**March 1938**); **Munich Agreement** (**September 1938**) gave Germany the **Sudetenland**, without Czechoslovakia or the USSR at the table; rest of **Czechoslovakia** occupied (**March 1939**).
- **End:** Britain and France then guaranteed **Poland**.

key_terms.definition_md: Giving way to an aggressor's demands to keep the peace.
The union of Austria with Germany in March 1938.

nodes.label: September 1938: Munich gives the Sudetenland to Germany

visual.alt: Flow of appeasement: the Rhineland remilitarised in 1936 with no action; the Anschluss in March 1938; Munich giving the Sudetenland to Germany in September 1938; the rest of Czechoslovakia occupied in March 1939; Britain and France then guarantee Poland
visual.caption: Each step encouraged the next.

sections.heading: 3. Aggression in Asia and Africa; the League fails
sections.body_md:
- **Manchuria (1931):** seized by Japan; condemned by the League; Japan **left** the League in **1933**.
- **Abyssinia (1935):** invaded by Italy; League **sanctions** were weak and excluded **oil**.
- **China (1937):** full-scale Japanese war.
- The League had **no army**, and Britain and France would not use force; **collective security** collapsed.

key_terms.definition_md: Penalties, such as trade bans, imposed on a state that breaks the rules.

visual.alt: Table of the League's failures: Manchuria in 1931, where Japan was condemned and left the League in 1933; Abyssinia in 1935, where Italy faced weak sanctions without an oil ban and completed its conquest; and China in 1937, where the League took no effective action

sections.heading: 4. The immediate cause
sections.body_md:
- **23 August 1939:** Nazi-Soviet **Non-Aggression Pact**; Hitler no longer feared a two-front war.
- **1 September 1939:** Germany **invaded Poland**.
- **3 September 1939:** Britain and France **declared war** on Germany.

key_terms.definition_md: An agreement between two states not to attack each other.

sections.heading: 5. A world war and its end
sections.body_md:
- **Pearl Harbour (7 December 1941):** Japan attacked the American naval base; the **USA** entered the war.
- **Germany** surrendered in **May 1945**.
- Atomic bombs on **Hiroshima (6 August)** and **Nagasaki (9 August 1945)** caused very heavy loss of life; **Japan** surrendered soon after.
- **Consequences:** Axis defeated; **United Nations** from **24 October 1945**; the **USA** and **USSR** became **superpowers**; Britain and France weakened.

key_terms.definition_md: A state with far greater military and economic power than others; after 1945, the USA and the USSR.

sections.heading: 6. The Cold War
sections.body_md:
- **Meaning:** the rivalry between the **USA** and the **USSR** after 1945, carried on through **alliances**, an **arms race** and **propaganda**, without a direct full-scale war between them.
- **NATO (1949):** military alliance of the USA, Canada and western European states for mutual defence.
- **Warsaw Pact (1955):** military alliance of the USSR and the communist states of eastern Europe.
- Only the **meaning** of NATO and the Warsaw Pact is required.

key_terms.definition_md: Superpower rivalry without direct war between the two sides.
Competition between states to build more and stronger weapons.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling the invasion of Poland the **only** cause (it was the **immediate** cause).
- Mixing up the **Anschluss** (Austria) and **Munich** (the Sudetenland).
- Writing that the League **fought** Japan or Italy (it had no army).
- Putting the USSR in **NATO** (it led the **Warsaw Pact**).
- Dating the United Nations to **1919** or **1920** (that was the League).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option or term.
- 2 marks: two distinct points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one point per mark; the 4-mark part often asks you to explain or evaluate.

**1936**: Italy and Germany; Japan joined later.
Giving way to an aggressor's demands to avoid war.
Invaded by Italy, **1935**; weak sanctions, no oil ban.
No army; members unwilling to use force.

questions.stem_md: Which grievance about the peace of 1919 did Hitler use most to win German support in the 1930s?

options.text_md: That Germany had been given too many colonies
That the Treaty of Versailles had humiliated Germany through war guilt, reparations and lost territory
That the treaty had made Germany's army too large
That Germany had been forced to join the League of Nations in 1919

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** That the Treaty of Versailles had humiliated Germany through war guilt, reparations and lost territory. Many Germans resented the war-guilt clause, reparations and loss of land, and Hitler promised to overturn the treaty. Germany lost its colonies, its army was cut, and it was kept out of the League at first.

questions.stem_md: How did the rise of Fascism in Italy and Nazism in Germany add to the danger of a second world war?

options.text_md: Both regimes reduced their armies to the minimum
Both regimes worked closely with the League to settle disputes
Both regimes gave up all claims to colonies
Both regimes glorified force and sought to expand their territory

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both regimes glorified force and sought to expand their territory. Mussolini and Hitler praised war and national expansion, rearmed and pursued conquests. The other options describe the opposite of their policies.

questions.stem_md: In the 1930s, Britain and France gave in to some of Hitler's demands in the hope of avoiding war. This policy is called
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** appeasement. Appeasement meant satisfying an aggressive power's demands to keep the peace. Collective security was the League's principle; non-alignment and containment belong to the Cold War period.

questions.stem_md: In which year did German troops march into the demilitarised Rhineland, breaking the Treaty of Versailles?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 1936. Germany remilitarised the Rhineland in March 1936. Britain and France protested but took no action, an early example of appeasement.

questions.stem_md: What was the Anschluss of March 1938?

options.text_md: The German occupation of the Rhineland
The handing over of the Sudetenland to Germany
The union of Austria with Germany, which the Treaty of Versailles had forbidden

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The union of Austria with Germany, which the Treaty of Versailles had forbidden. Anschluss means union: Germany annexed Austria in March 1938, though the peace treaties had forbidden it. The Rhineland was 1936, the Sudetenland followed in September 1938, and Poland in 1939.

questions.stem_md: The Munich Agreement of September 1938 allowed Germany to take over which area?

options.text_md: The Sudetenland, a German-speaking border region of Czechoslovakia

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Sudetenland, a German-speaking border region of Czechoslovakia. At Munich, Britain, France, Germany and Italy agreed that Germany could take the Sudetenland from Czechoslovakia. Czechoslovakia itself was not consulted.

questions.stem_md: Which four powers took part in the Munich Agreement of 1938?

options.text_md: Britain, France, the USSR and Czechoslovakia
Germany, Italy, Japan and the USSR
Britain, the USA, France and Poland

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Britain, France, Germany and Italy. The leaders of Britain, France, Germany and Italy met at Munich. Neither Czechoslovakia nor the USSR was invited, which deepened Soviet distrust of the western powers.

questions.stem_md: Why is Germany's occupation of the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939 seen as the end of appeasement?

options.text_md: It was approved by the League of Nations
It showed that Hitler's aims went beyond German-speaking lands, so Britain and France promised to defend Poland
It returned the Sudetenland to Czechoslovakia
It ended the Treaty of Versailles by agreement

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It showed that Hitler's aims went beyond German-speaking lands, so Britain and France promised to defend Poland. By taking non-German lands, Hitler broke his Munich promise. Britain and France now guaranteed Poland's independence, abandoning appeasement. The League did not approve it, and the Sudetenland was not returned.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Munich Agreement encouraged Hitler to make further demands.

**Reason (R):** At Munich, Britain and France gave in to Hitler's claim to the Sudetenland without a fight.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: seeing that Britain and France would yield, Hitler expected further gains without war, and he soon occupied the rest of Czechoslovakia and turned to Poland.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Many Germans wanted the Treaty of Versailles to be overturned.

**Reason (R):** The League of Nations had its headquarters at Geneva.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. German resentment came from war guilt, reparations and lost land; the League's location has nothing to do with it.

questions.stem_md: True or false? When German troops entered the Rhineland in 1936, Britain and France sent their armies to drive them out.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Britain and France protested but took no military action, which encouraged Hitler to take further steps.

questions.stem_md: Give two ways in which German resentment of the 1919 peace settlement prepared the ground for the war of 1939.
questions.solution_md: Two linked points: resentment and its use by Hitler.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **war-guilt** clause, **reparations** and loss of **land** made many Germans want the treaty **overturned**.
2. **Hitler** used this anger to win support, then broke the treaty by **rearming** and seizing territory.

marking_scheme.step: Hitler used it to break the treaty

questions.stem_md: State two reasons why Britain and France followed a policy of appeasement towards Germany.
questions.solution_md: Any two reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Memories of the **First World War** made people afraid of another war, and the two countries were **not ready** to fight.
2. Some leaders thought Germany's grievances over **Versailles** were partly **fair** and saw Germany as a barrier to **communism**.

questions.stem_md: How did the friendship between Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany change the balance of power in Europe in the 1930s?
questions.solution_md: The Axis and its effect.

answer.model_answer_md: Italy and Germany drew together in the **Rome–Berlin Axis** of **1936**, later joined by **Japan**. This created a group of **aggressive powers** acting together against the **League** and the western democracies.

marking_scheme.step: Effect on the balance of power

questions.stem_md: Describe three steps between 1936 and 1938 at which Britain and France allowed Germany to break the Treaty of Versailles.
questions.solution_md: Rhineland; Anschluss; Munich.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **1936:** German troops entered the **demilitarised Rhineland**, and Britain and France only protested.
2. **March 1938:** Germany annexed **Austria** (the **Anschluss**), which had been forbidden, without resistance.
3. **September 1938:** at **Munich**, Britain and France agreed that Germany could take the **Sudetenland** from Czechoslovakia.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the European causes of the Second World War.

(i) How did the Treaty of Versailles leave Germany dissatisfied? **[3]**
(ii) How did the rise of Fascism and Nazism threaten peace? **[3]**
(iii) Explain how the policy of appeasement made a general war more likely. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Versailles; dictatorships; appeasement and its results.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Germany had to accept **war guilt** and pay **reparations**, lost **Alsace-Lorraine**, the **Polish Corridor** and its colonies, and its **army** was cut to a small force. Germans saw it as a **dictated** peace and wanted it overturned.

(ii) **Mussolini** in Italy and **Hitler** in Germany set up dictatorships that **glorified force**. They **rearmed**, rejected the League, and sought **new territory**; in 1936 they drew together in the **Rome–Berlin Axis**.

(iii) Britain and France let Hitler **remilitarise the Rhineland** (1936), annex **Austria** (March 1938) and take the **Sudetenland** at **Munich** (September 1938). Each success **strengthened** Germany and convinced Hitler that the democracies would **not fight**, so he went on to occupy the rest of Czechoslovakia and to demand Polish territory. When he invaded **Poland**, Britain and France could no longer give way.

questions.stem_md:
With reference to the years 1936 to 1939, answer the following.

(i) What was meant by appeasement, and which two countries followed it? **[3]**
(ii) What did the Munich Agreement of 1938 decide, and who was left out of the talks? **[3]**
(iii) Give arguments on both sides: did appeasement buy time for peace, or did it make war certain? **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Meaning; Munich; balanced evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Appeasement meant **giving in** to some of an aggressor's demands in the hope of **avoiding war**. It was followed mainly by **Britain** and **France** towards Hitler's Germany in the late 1930s.

(ii) At **Munich** in **September 1938**, Britain, France, Germany and Italy agreed that Germany could take the **Sudetenland**, a German-speaking region of **Czechoslovakia**. **Czechoslovakia** itself and the **USSR** were not part of the talks.

(iii) **For buying time:** Britain and France were not ready for war in 1938, and the delay let them **rearm**; public opinion still feared a repeat of 1914–18. **For making war certain:** each concession **strengthened** Germany and taught Hitler that the democracies would **not resist**; it lost **Czechoslovakia** as an ally and made the USSR **distrust** the West. A balanced conclusion is that appeasement **delayed** war but on worse terms for the democracies.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Czechoslovakia and the USSR left out

questions.stem_md: In which year did Japan invade Manchuria, a province of China?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 1931. Japan seized Manchuria in 1931. It launched a full-scale war on China in 1937 and attacked Pearl Harbour in 1941.

questions.stem_md: How did Japan respond when the League of Nations condemned its occupation of Manchuria?

options.text_md: It returned Manchuria to China at once
It left the League in 1933 and kept Manchuria
It asked the League to send an army

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It left the League in 1933 and kept Manchuria. Japan walked out of the League in 1933 and kept Manchuria. The League could only condemn; it had no army, which exposed its weakness.

questions.stem_md: An imagined newspaper of 1937 reports that the power which had seized a north-eastern province of China six years earlier has now launched a full-scale war on the whole of China. Which power and which province are meant?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Japan; Manchuria. Japan seized Manchuria in 1931 and began its full-scale war on China in 1937, six years later. The other pairs are aggressions in Africa or Europe.

questions.stem_md: Which country did Mussolini's Italy invade in 1935, testing the League of Nations once again?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Abyssinia (Ethiopia). Italy invaded Abyssinia in October 1935. The League's economic sanctions were limited and did not stop the conquest.

questions.stem_md: Why did the League's sanctions against Italy over Abyssinia fail to stop the invasion?

options.text_md: Italy was not a member of the League
The League sent an army that was defeated
The USA enforced them too strictly
They did not cover vital goods such as oil and were not firmly enforced by the leading members

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** They did not cover vital goods such as oil and were not firmly enforced by the leading members. The sanctions left out key goods like oil, and Britain and France did not want to push Italy into war or into Germany's arms. The League had no army, and the USA was not a member.

questions.stem_md: Which agreement, signed on 23 August 1939, cleared the way for Germany's attack on Poland?

options.text_md: The Nazi-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact between Germany and the USSR

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Nazi-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact between Germany and the USSR. In the Non-Aggression Pact, Germany and the USSR promised not to fight each other, so Hitler no longer feared a war on two fronts. Munich was 1938; the North Atlantic Treaty came in 1949.

questions.stem_md: On which date did Germany invade Poland, the immediate cause of the Second World War?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 1 September 1939. Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. Britain and France declared war on 3 September; the Nazi-Soviet Pact was signed on 23 August; Pearl Harbour was attacked on 7 December 1941.

questions.stem_md: Britain and France declared war on Germany two days after the invasion of Poland. On which date was this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 3 September 1939. They declared war on 3 September 1939, two days after the invasion began on 1 September.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The League of Nations failed to stop Japan in Manchuria and Italy in Abyssinia.

**Reason (R):** The League had no army of its own and its leading members were unwilling to use force.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: without an army and without firm action by Britain and France, the League could only protest and impose weak sanctions.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Britain and France declared war on Germany in September 1939.

**Reason (R):** Germany had attacked Britain directly in August 1939.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true. R is false: Germany had not attacked Britain; Britain and France declared war because Germany invaded Poland, whose independence they had promised to defend.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the 1930s the League of Nations used its own army to drive Japan out of Manchuria.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. The League had no army. It condemned Japan, which left the League in 1933 and kept Manchuria.

questions.stem_md: State two acts of Japanese aggression in China during the 1930s and how the League responded.
questions.solution_md: Two acts with the League's response.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Japan seized **Manchuria** in **1931**; the League **condemned** it, and Japan **left the League** in **1933**.
2. Japan began a **full-scale war** on **China** in **1937**, and the League took **no effective action**.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why the failure of the League of Nations in the 1930s encouraged aggressive states.
questions.solution_md: Two reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Aggressors like **Japan** and **Italy** saw that the League could only **protest**, since it had **no army**.
2. Its leading members **Britain** and **France** would not act firmly, so **collective security** collapsed.

questions.stem_md: Why did the Non-Aggression Pact between Germany and the USSR in August 1939 make an attack on Poland easier for Hitler?
questions.solution_md: Removed the danger of a two-front war.

answer.model_answer_md: Hitler no longer feared that the **USSR** would fight him in the **east** while Britain and France fought in the **west**. Germany could invade **Poland** without the risk of a **two-front war**.

questions.stem_md: Explain three steps by which the crisis over Poland turned into a general war in 1939.
questions.solution_md: Pact; invasion; declarations.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Germany and the **USSR** signed a **Non-Aggression Pact** on **23 August 1939**, freeing Hitler from fear of the east.
2. **Germany invaded Poland** on **1 September 1939**.
3. **Britain and France**, which had promised to defend Poland, **declared war** on Germany on **3 September 1939**.

questions.stem_md:
With reference to aggression in Asia and Africa in the 1930s, answer the following.

(i) Describe Japan's aggression against China between 1931 and 1937. **[3]**
(ii) How did Italy challenge the League over Abyssinia? **[3]**
(iii) Explain how the failure of the League in these crises helped to bring about the Second World War. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Japan; Italy; why the League's failure mattered.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) In **1931** Japan seized **Manchuria**, a resource-rich province of **China**. When the League condemned this, Japan **left the League** in **1933** and kept the territory. In **1937** Japan began a **full-scale war** against China.

(ii) In **1935** Mussolini's Italy invaded **Abyssinia** (Ethiopia), a fellow member of the League. The League imposed **economic sanctions**, but they left out **oil** and were weakly enforced, and Italy completed its conquest.

(iii) The League had **no army** and depended on its members, but **Britain** and **France** would not use force. Its failure showed aggressors that they could **break the rules** without punishment, destroyed faith in **collective security**, and drew **Japan**, **Italy** and **Germany** closer together. Each unpunished act of aggression encouraged the next, ending in the attack on **Poland** in **1939**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the outbreak of war in 1939.

(i) What was the Nazi-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact, and why was it signed? **[3]**
(ii) Describe the immediate cause of the Second World War. **[3]**
(iii) Why could Britain and France no longer follow appeasement in 1939? **[4]**
questions.solution_md: The pact; Poland; end of appeasement.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) On **23 August 1939** Germany and the **USSR** agreed **not to attack** each other. Hitler wanted to avoid a **war on two fronts** before attacking Poland; Stalin, distrustful of Britain and France after **Munich**, wanted time and safety.

(ii) On **1 September 1939** Germany **invaded Poland**. Britain and France had promised to defend Poland, so on **3 September 1939** they **declared war** on Germany, and the Second World War began.

(iii) In **March 1939** Hitler had occupied the rest of **Czechoslovakia**, breaking his **Munich** promise and showing that his aims went far beyond German-speaking lands. British and French leaders now saw that concessions only **encouraged** him, public opinion had turned against **giving way**, and they had **guaranteed Poland's** independence. To keep their word and stop further conquests, they had to **fight**.

questions.stem_md: On which date did Japan attack the American naval base at Pearl Harbour?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 7 December 1941. Japan attacked Pearl Harbour, in Hawaii, on 7 December 1941. The other dates are the invasion of Poland, the bombing of Hiroshima and the founding of the United Nations.

questions.stem_md: What was the most important result of the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbour?

options.text_md: The League of Nations was revived
The United States entered the war against Japan and its Axis partners

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The United States entered the war against Japan and its Axis partners. The attack brought the USA into the war, turning a European and Asian conflict into a truly world war.

questions.stem_md: On which dates were atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 6 August and 9 August 1945. The USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 and on Nagasaki on 9 August 1945, three days apart.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Indian soldier serving in Burma writes home in late August 1945 that the fighting in Asia has suddenly stopped, only days after two enemy cities were destroyed by a new kind of bomb. What had happened?

options.text_md: Germany surrendered for the first time
Japan announced its surrender, ending the war in Asia
The League of Nations was founded

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Japan announced its surrender, ending the war in Asia. Japan announced its surrender in August 1945 and signed it in early September. Germany had already surrendered in May 1945, and the League dated from 1920.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The USA joined the Second World War in December 1941.

**Reason (R):** Japan attacked the American naval base at Pearl Harbour on 7 December 1941.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: the surprise attack led the USA to declare war on Japan, and Germany and Italy then declared war on the USA.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the two cities struck by atomic bombs in 1945, are in Japan.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. Both are Japanese cities; the bombings caused very heavy loss of life and lasting suffering from radiation.

questions.stem_md: Write two consequences of the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbour in December 1941.
questions.solution_md: Two consequences.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **USA** declared war on **Japan** and, with Germany and Italy declaring war on it, joined the **Allies**.
2. The war became a truly **world war**, fought across **Europe**, **Asia** and the **Pacific**.

questions.stem_md: Why are the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki seen as a turning point in world history? Give two reasons.
questions.solution_md: End of the war; nuclear age.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. They brought the war in **Asia** to a quick end, as **Japan** surrendered within days.
2. They showed the terrible power of **nuclear weapons**, causing very heavy **loss of life**, and began the **nuclear age** and arms race.

questions.stem_md: An imagined London diary entry of May 1945 records crowds celebrating in the streets because the war in Europe is over, although fighting still goes on in Asia. What event are they celebrating?

options.text_md: The founding of the United Nations

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The unconditional surrender of Germany. Germany surrendered unconditionally in May 1945, ending the war in Europe. Japan surrendered only in August–September 1945, and the United Nations came into existence in October 1945.

questions.stem_md: The United Nations came into existence after the Second World War on which date?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 24 October 1945. The UN came into existence on 24 October 1945. The League began work in January 1920, and NATO was founded in April 1949.

questions.stem_md: Which two countries emerged from the Second World War as the world's leading powers, often called superpowers?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The USA and the USSR. The war weakened Britain and France and defeated Germany, Italy and Japan; the USA and the USSR emerged as the two superpowers.

questions.stem_md: Which three powers formed the Axis that was defeated in the Second World War?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Germany, Italy and Japan. The Axis powers were Germany, Italy and Japan. Britain, France, the USSR, the USA and China were among the Allies.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The United Nations was set up in 1945.

**Reason (R):** The League of Nations had failed to prevent a second world war.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: the League's failure led the Allies to create a stronger international body to keep the peace after the war.

questions.stem_md: Mention two political consequences of the Second World War for the world.
questions.solution_md: Any two consequences.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **Axis** powers, **Germany**, **Italy** and **Japan**, were **defeated**, and Germany was occupied and later divided.
2. The **United Nations** was formed in **1945**, and the **USA** and **USSR** emerged as **superpowers**.

questions.stem_md: Explain three ways in which the world after 1945 was different from the world before the Second World War.
questions.solution_md: Three changes.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Britain** and **France** were weakened, while the **USA** and the **USSR** became **superpowers**.
2. A new body, the **United Nations**, replaced the failed **League of Nations**.
3. Rivalry between the two superpowers began the **Cold War**, dividing much of the world into two **blocs**.

questions.stem_md:
With reference to the end of the Second World War, answer the following.

(i) How did the war end in Europe and in Asia? **[3]**
(ii) State three consequences of the war for the world order. **[3]**
(iii) Explain how the war led to the Cold War between the USA and the USSR. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: End of the war; consequences; origin of the Cold War.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) In Europe, **Germany** surrendered unconditionally in **May 1945**. In Asia, after the USA dropped atomic bombs on **Hiroshima** (**6 August**) and **Nagasaki** (**9 August 1945**), **Japan** announced its surrender, which was signed in early **September 1945**.

(ii) The **Axis** powers were **defeated**; the **United Nations** came into existence on **24 October 1945**; and the **USA** and the **USSR** emerged as **superpowers**, while Britain and France were weakened.

(iii) The two superpowers had been **allies** only against a common enemy. After the war their **ideologies** clashed: the USA stood for **capitalism** and multi-party democracy, the USSR for **communism**. Each **distrusted** the other, especially over **Eastern Europe**, which came under Soviet influence, and each built up **nuclear** and other weapons. This rivalry, fought through **alliances**, an **arms race** and propaganda rather than direct war, became the **Cold War**.

questions.stem_md: Why was the rivalry between the USA and the USSR after 1945 called a cold war?

options.text_md: The two superpowers competed through alliances, an arms race and propaganda without fighting each other directly
It was fought only in the polar regions
It was a war that took place in winter

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The two superpowers competed through alliances, an arms race and propaganda without fighting each other directly. Cold means there was no direct full-scale war between the two superpowers; they competed through alliances, weapons and propaganda.

questions.stem_md: NATO, formed in 1949, was

options.text_md: an alliance of the USSR and eastern European states
a military alliance of the USA and western European countries for mutual defence
an agency of the United Nations for health

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a military alliance of the USA and western European countries for mutual defence. The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (1949) joined the USA, Canada and western European countries, promising to defend one another. The Warsaw Pact was the Soviet-led alliance.

questions.stem_md: An imagined factory newsletter from Poland in 1955 announces that the country has joined a new military alliance led by the Soviet Union and signed in the Polish capital. Which alliance is meant?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Warsaw Pact. The Warsaw Pact of 1955, named after the Polish capital, joined the USSR and the communist states of eastern Europe. NATO was the western alliance.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Canadian sailor writes in 1950 that his country joined, the year before, an alliance with the USA and western Europe in which an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all. Which alliance is it?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation. NATO was formed in April 1949 by the USA, Canada and western European countries for mutual defence. The Warsaw Pact was the Soviet-led alliance of 1955.

questions.stem_md: An imagined cartoon of late August 1939 shows two dictators who had long attacked each other in speeches now shaking hands over a map of the country lying between them. What does the cartoon show?

options.text_md: The Munich Agreement over the Sudetenland
The Rome-Berlin Axis between Italy and Germany
The Nazi-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact, which left Poland exposed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Nazi-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact, which left Poland exposed. Germany and the USSR, long hostile, signed the Non-Aggression Pact on 23 August 1939; Poland lay between them and was invaded on 1 September. Munich (1938) and the Axis (1936) came earlier.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined case of 1956, a newly independent country receives offers of loans and weapons from both superpowers, each hoping to win it as a friend. Which feature of the Cold War does this show?

options.text_md: Competition between the two blocs for allies and influence

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Competition between the two blocs for allies and influence. Both superpowers used aid and arms to win friends among new nations; this competition for influence was a key feature of the Cold War.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Abyssinian envoy writes to the League in 1936 that its sanctions on Italy shut the front door but left the back door open. Explain what the envoy means.
questions.solution_md: Weak sanctions; conquest completed.

answer.model_answer_md: The sanctions banned some trade but **left out oil** and other vital goods, so Italy could still supply its armies. Because members did not **enforce** them firmly, Italy **completed** its conquest of Abyssinia.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Cold War divided much of the world into two rival blocs.

**Reason (R):** The United Nations came into existence in 1945.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. The blocs grew from the rivalry and distrust between the USA and the USSR, not from the founding of the United Nations.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Warsaw Pact was an alliance led by the United States.

**Reason (R):** The Warsaw Pact was formed in 1955.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false: the Warsaw Pact was led by the USSR. R is true: it was formed in 1955.

questions.stem_md: True or false? During the Cold War, the armies of the USA and the USSR fought a full-scale war directly against each other.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. The two superpowers never fought each other directly in a full-scale war; they competed through alliances, an arms race and propaganda.

questions.stem_md: The military alliance formed in 1955 by the USSR and the communist countries of eastern Europe was called the ___ Pact.
questions.solution_md: It was the Warsaw Pact.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the Cold War? Name the two powers that led it.
questions.solution_md: Meaning; the two powers.

answer.model_answer_md: The Cold War was the long **rivalry** after **1945** in which the two sides competed through **alliances**, an **arms race** and **propaganda**, without fighting each other **directly**. It was led by the **USA** and the **USSR**.

questions.stem_md: What were NATO and the Warsaw Pact? State the year in which each was formed.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and year of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **NATO** (**1949**) was a **military alliance** of the **USA** and western countries for mutual defence. The **Warsaw Pact** (**1955**) was the rival alliance of the **USSR** and the **communist** states of eastern Europe.

questions.stem_md: How did the formation of NATO and then the Warsaw Pact deepen the division between East and West?
questions.solution_md: Rival armed blocs; arms race.

answer.model_answer_md: Each alliance bound its members to **defend** one another, so Europe was split into two armed **blocs** facing each other. Fear of the other bloc led to an **arms race** and deeper **suspicion**.

questions.stem_md:
With reference to the Cold War, answer the following.

(i) What is meant by the Cold War, and why did it begin after 1945? **[3]**
(ii) What were NATO and the Warsaw Pact? **[3]**
(iii) Evaluate how the Cold War affected the newly independent countries of Asia and Africa. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Meaning and origin; the two alliances; effect on new nations.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The Cold War was the rivalry between the **USA** and the **USSR** in which they competed through **alliances**, an **arms race** and **propaganda** without fighting each other directly. It began because their **ideologies** clashed, capitalism against **communism**, and each **distrusted** the other after the war, especially over **Eastern Europe**.

(ii) **NATO** (**1949**) was a **military alliance** of the **USA**, **Canada** and western European countries for **mutual defence**. The **Warsaw Pact** (**1955**) was the rival military alliance of the **USSR** and the communist states of **eastern Europe**.

(iii) Both blocs tried to win **new nations** as allies, offering **aid** and **weapons**. This brought **pressure** on new states to take sides and sometimes drew them into **conflicts**. On the other hand, the rivalry let them seek **help** from both sides, and many, including **India**, chose to stay **non-aligned**, keeping their freedom of action while working for **peace**.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **1931:** Japan seized **Manchuria**. **1935:** Italy invaded **Abyssinia**. **1936:** Germany remilitarised the **Rhineland** (and in **1938** annexed **Austria** and took the **Sudetenland**).

(ii) **20 years** (1939 − 1919). Historians link them because German **resentment** of the treaty's **war guilt**, **reparations** and lost land helped **Hitler** rise to power and win support for overturning it by force.

assets.caption: Cold War blocs in Europe (schematic, drawn by SOYL; members shown are examples only).

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **Western bloc**, led by the **USA**, with **NATO** (**1949**); and the **Eastern bloc**, led by the **USSR**, with the **Warsaw Pact** (**1955**).

(ii) The USA and the USSR had fought together only against a **common enemy**. After the war their **ideologies** clashed, **capitalism** against **communism**; the West feared Soviet influence in **Eastern Europe**, and the USSR feared the West's **atomic** power and its support for western Europe.

(iii) There was an **arms race** in nuclear and other weapons; each side spread **propaganda** against the other; the superpowers competed for **allies** among new nations with **aid**; and they sometimes backed opposite sides in **local conflicts** while avoiding a direct war with each other.

questions.passage_md:
**Diary of an imagined newspaper typist in London, autumn 1938**

The crowds outside the office cheered today when the news came from the Bavarian city: the four leaders have agreed, and the German-speaking border lands of the young central European republic will pass to Germany. My editor did not cheer. He said that the republic whose land was given away had not even been asked, and that each time we give way the man in Berlin simply asks for more. My brother, who fought in the last war, said only that he was glad his son would not have to.

children.stem_md: Name the agreement the crowds were cheering and the region it handed over.

answer.model_answer_md: The **Munich Agreement** (1938); the **Sudetenland**.

children.stem_md: Which country is the young central European republic that had not been asked?

answer.model_answer_md: **Czechoslovakia**.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Which policy does the editor criticise, and what danger does he see in it?

answer.model_answer_md: **Appeasement**. He fears that each **concession** only **encourages** Hitler to make **further demands**, as happened when Germany took the rest of Czechoslovakia in 1939.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Why might the brother, a soldier of the last war, have supported the agreement? Give two reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: He remembered the terrible **suffering** of **1914–18** and wanted to **avoid** another war; many people also felt Britain was **not ready** to fight in 1938.

questions.passage_md:
**Letter from an imagined clerk in Singapore to his sister in Madras, mid-December 1941**

The wireless here talks of nothing else. Last Sunday morning aircraft of the empire that has been fighting in China for four years struck the great American fleet at its island base in the Pacific. The Americans, who had stayed out of the war for over two years, are now in it. Our office manager says the war has become truly worldwide, and that the fighting may soon reach these shores.

children.stem_md: Name the attack described and the country that carried it out.

answer.model_answer_md: The attack on **Pearl Harbour** (7 December 1941), carried out by **Japan**.

children.stem_md: In which year had this empire begun its full-scale war in China, about four years before the letter?
**Either** (i): Why does the office manager say the war has become truly worldwide?

answer.model_answer_md: With the **USA** now fighting **Japan**, and Germany and Italy at war with the USA, the war spread across **Europe**, **Asia** and the **Pacific**, involving all the major powers.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): The letter says the Americans had stayed out for over two years. When had the war begun in Europe, and what event began it?

answer.model_answer_md: On **1 September 1939**, when **Germany invaded Poland**; Britain and France declared war two days later.

questions.stem_md: Read the extract from the imagined notes of a student and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people in it are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** The two superpowers.

**(b)** NATO; Warsaw Pact.

**(c) (i)** No direct war; arms race and rivalry.

**OR (c) (ii)** One advantage, one risk.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **USA** and the **USSR**.

**(b)** **NATO** (formed **1949**) and the **Warsaw Pact** (**1955**).

**(c) (i)** There was **no direct war** between the two superpowers; instead they competed through an **arms race** and rivalry for **allies** and influence.

**OR (c) (ii)** **Advantage:** it kept its **freedom** to decide its own policies and could seek help from both sides. **Risk:** it might face **pressure** from both blocs and lack the protection of an alliance.

questions.passage_md:
**Notes of an imagined Indian college student at a public lecture in Delhi, 1956**

The speaker said the world had escaped one great war only to fall into a long quarrel of a new kind. The two giants that defeated the Axis now distrust each other. One leads an alliance of western countries formed seven years ago; the other answered last year with an alliance of its own in eastern Europe. They do not fight each other directly, but they race to build weapons and compete for friends. He said that new nations like ours need not join either camp.

children.stem_md: Name the two giants the speaker refers to.

answer.model_answer_md: The **USA** and the **USSR**.

children.stem_md: Name the two alliances described in the notes.

answer.model_answer_md: **NATO** (formed **1949**) and the **Warsaw Pact** (**1955**).

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Why is this quarrel of a new kind called the Cold War? Use two features from the notes.
children.solution_md: No direct war; arms race and rivalry.

answer.model_answer_md: There was **no direct war** between the two superpowers; instead they competed through an **arms race** and rivalry for **allies** and influence.

questions.stem_md: An imagined German poster of 1936 shows soldiers crossing a bridge over a great western river, with the words 'our own land again'. Which event does it celebrate?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The remilitarisation of the Rhineland. German troops entered the demilitarised Rhineland in 1936, breaking the Treaty of Versailles. Poland, Munich and Pearl Harbour came later.

questions.stem_md: An imagined radio broadcast in London on a Sunday morning in September 1939 tells listeners that the country is now at war because a promise to an eastern European ally has been broken. Which ally is meant?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Poland. Britain declared war on 3 September 1939 because Germany had invaded Poland, whose independence Britain had guaranteed.

questions.stem_md: A student's imagined sketch map of Europe in 1938 shades Austria in the same colour as Germany. Which event does the shading show?

options.text_md: The Munich Agreement over the Sudetenland

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Anschluss of March 1938. Austria joined to Germany shows the Anschluss of March 1938. Munich concerned the Sudetenland of Czechoslovakia.

questions.stem_md: An imagined shipping clerk in 1936 notes that oil tankers are still sailing to an Italian port even though Italy is under League sanctions. What does this show about the League's response to the Abyssinian crisis?

options.text_md: The League had forbidden all trade with Italy
The League had sent its army to Abyssinia
The sanctions left out vital goods such as oil and were too weak to stop Italy

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The sanctions left out vital goods such as oil and were too weak to stop Italy. Oil was not included in the sanctions, so Italy could continue its war. The League had no army.

questions.stem_md: An imagined news report of 1953 says that each of two rival powers has tested a more powerful bomb, and that each fears falling behind the other. Which feature of the Cold War does this show?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The arms race. Competing to build ever more powerful weapons was the arms race, a central feature of the Cold War.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined school debate in 1946, a student argues that the world needs a stronger body than the one that failed in the 1930s. Which organisation, just founded, is she supporting?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The United Nations. The United Nations, founded on 24 October 1945, replaced the League of Nations, which had failed to prevent the war.

questions.stem_md: A student writes that the invasion of Poland alone caused the Second World War. Correct this view in two points.
questions.solution_md: Immediate versus long-term causes.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The invasion of **Poland** was only the **immediate cause**.
2. The **long-term causes** were already present: resentment of **Versailles**, the rise of **Fascism** and **Nazism**, **appeasement**, Japanese aggression and the **failure** of the League.

questions.stem_md: Which agreement of 1936 brought Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany together?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Rome-Berlin Axis. The Rome-Berlin Axis of 1936 linked Italy and Germany; Japan later joined them.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Under the Munich Agreement of 1938, Germany was allowed to take the Sudetenland.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. Britain, France, Germany and Italy agreed to hand the Sudetenland to Germany.

questions.stem_md: The Second World War began when Germany invaded ___ on 1 September 1939.
questions.solution_md: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939.

questions.stem_md: Which country invaded Abyssinia in 1935?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Italy. Mussolini's Italy invaded Abyssinia in 1935.

questions.stem_md: The attack on Pearl Harbour in 1941 was carried out by
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Japan. Japan attacked the American base at Pearl Harbour on 7 December 1941.

questions.stem_md: The United Nations came into existence on 24 October ___.
questions.solution_md: The United Nations came into existence on 24 October 1945.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The USSR was a member of NATO.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. NATO was the western alliance led by the USA; the USSR led the rival Warsaw Pact.

questions.stem_md: On which Japanese city was the first atomic bomb dropped, on 6 August 1945?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Hiroshima. The first atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945; the second on Nagasaki on 9 August.
